The claim states that the evidence supports the strategy of keeping track of the pose used for replacement for each erroneous viewpoint and skipping poses that have already been utilized to prevent redundant erroneous replacements and optimization stagnation. Source [S1] explicitly mentions in the notes and the passage: 'Apply replacement-memory technique: keep track of the pose used for replacement for each erroneous viewpoint and skip poses that have already been utilized to prevent redundant erroneous replacements.' and 'Hence, we introduce a replacement-memory technique to prevent redundant erroneous replacements. Non-maxima suppression mitigates this [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] passages that 'we incorporate non-maxima suppression [19]–[21] to enhance the identification of inaccurate poses.' It further explains that this technique is used to address the issue where accurate poses might be mistakenly labeled as low-quality due to interference from neighboring inaccurate poses. By discarding misidentified low-scoring poses when multiple neighbors have low scores, non-maxima suppression improves the accuracy of identifying which poses are actually inaccurate (mitigating the problem of false positives in pose identification, which is the context of 'S1' referring to the identification/replacement strategy). Therefore, the claim that non-maxima suppression mitigates the issues associated with the strategy described in S1 is supported by the text.
